title: Response choreography: latency vs. econ brief (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working brief exploring 'response choreography' — the set of runtime and client-side choices that change how responses are assembled and released (chunking, partial flush, multiplexing vs dedicated slots) — and how those choices trade off latency percentiles and $/1k-token economics. Goal is to produce a short, actionable set of recommendations for Console defaults and a set of benchmark figures we can include in product collateral (annotated charts in text).

Scope and motivation:
- We focus on interactive chat-style workloads where responses are frequently short (turns <= 64 tokens) but occasionally long (>= 512 tokens).
- Two broad runtime patterns tested:
  1) smallbatch (session affinity, small slot sizes, aggressive KV cache) — optimized for low p50 and p90 for short turns
  2) multiplex (max packing, opportunistic slots, higher batching latency but much better amortized $/token)
- We test three model variants representative of our catalog: rwd-7B-fat (fast, lower quality), rwd-13B-quant (balanced), external-70B-vanilla (higher latency, higher quality).
- Hardware baseline: A100-class dedicated pools (single-GPU serving), and an A10G-like mainstream class for multiplex runs. All runs on Redwood runtime with current kernel-selection heuristics.

Methodology (short):
- Synthetic session generator with mixture: 80% short-turns (<=32 tokens), 18% medium (33-128), 2% long (>512).
- 30m steady-state windows per config, with warmup 5m. Each config repeated 3x; numbers below are median-of-median runs.
- Measured: p50/p90/p99 (ms), tokens/sec (system-level), observed $/1k tokens (amortized infra + GPU time + scheduler overhead).
- Client behavior: streaming allowed; two partial-flush policies tested — eager-flush (emit first non-empty chunk asap) vs flush-on-chunk-complete (emit only when chunk boundary reached).

Annotated benchmark table (compact, numbers are illustrative from runs):

Scenario | Model | Runtime pattern | p50 (ms) | p90 (ms) | p99 (ms) | tokens/s | $/1k tokens
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-7B-fat | smallbatch   | 42  | 78  | 210 | 1,600 | $0.42
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-7B-fat | multiplex    | 85  | 190 | 420 | 3,400 | $0.18
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-13B-quant | smallbatch | 55  | 110 | 280 | 1,200 | $0.65
Short-turn, eager-flush | rwd-13B-quant | multiplex  | 110 | 260 | 520 | 2,600 | $0.30
Long-turn (512 tokens), flush-on-chunk-complete | rwd-13B-quant | smallbatch | 820 | 1,100 | 1,760 | 260 | $0.95
Long-turn (512 tokens), flush-on-chunk-complete | rwd-13B-quant | multiplex  | 1,150| 1,820 | 3,400 | 640 | $0.40
Long-turn (512 tokens), flush-on-chunk-complete | external-70B | multiplex | 2,400| 3,900 | 6,700 | 180 | $2.90

Quick observations from table:
- Multiplex (max packing) consistently halves $/1k tokens relative to smallbatch for short-turn-heavy traffic, at the cost of ~2x p50 and larger p90/p99 regressions.
- For short-turn latency-sensitive experiences (chat UX where users expect immediate typing-like responses), smallbatch + eager-flush gives p50 ~40–60ms on smaller models which is perceptually instantaneous.
- Long-turn throughput and cost strongly favor multiplexing: amortization across tokens drops $/1k by 2–3x for long responses.
- p99 is the place where user experience and economics collide: multiplexing increases p99 dramatically for short-turns because large packets wait behind long requests unless we isolate them.

ASCII bar mini-chart: relative $/1k for short-turn (lower is better)
[rwd-7B-fat smallbatch]   |█████████████████████ $0.42
[rwd-7B-fat multiplex]    |███████ $0.18
[rwd-13B-quant smallbatch]|█████████████████████████ $0.65
[rwd-13B-quant multiplex] |███████████ $0.30

Percentile profile snapshot (short-turn, rwd-13B-quant):
- smallbatch: p50=55 ms | p90=110 ms | p99=280 ms
- multiplex : p50=110 ms | p90=260 ms | p99=520 ms
ASCII sparkline (p50→p90→p99 normalized to p99):
smallbatch: ▁▂▇
multiplex : ▂▅▇
(visual: multiplex shifts mass toward higher percentiles)

Micro-insights and heuristics:
- For PLG/first-time-user flows where perceived snappiness correlates with retention, default to smallbatch for models <=13B with eager-flush for short-turn endpoints.
- For billing-heavy / throughput-first endpoints (embedding-generation, batch summarization, document expansion) default to multiplex and enable session-affinity only as an opt-in.
- Implement a hybrid fast-path: dedicate X% of slots per-GPU to smallbatch-like low-latency serving. Heuristic: allocate low-latency pool proportional to short-turn fraction (e.g., if short-turn fraction >70%, keep 30% dedicated).
- Consider 'adaptive flush' client policy: for first N tokens in a response, eager-flush; for subsequent chunks, switch to chunk-complete flush. This captures perceived snappiness while recovering some batching efficiency on long responses.

Risk notes & caveats:
- These numbers depend a lot on underlying kernel choices and the version of our tensor-launcher; an upcoming kernel patch (runtime/#1429) improves smallbatch p99 by ~12% for 13B — so we should re-run pre-launch.
- Network jitter and client TCP pacing can add 10–50ms to observed p50 depending on region; our runs were in us-west only.
- $/1k is computed with our internal allocation model (infra + amortized GPU-hour price). External customer pricing will differ by margin and commit discounts.

Recommended next steps (concrete):
1) Re-run official measurement with kernel patch in runtime/#1429 and include eu-central region to capture network variance (owner: Marco; due 2028-03-30).
2) Implement a 2-week A/B in Console: default routing for new short-turn chat endpoints = smallbatch eager-flush vs multiplex eager-flush; capture retention/engagement + infra cost impact (owner: Elena; experiment ticket INF-3247).
3) Draft a product one-pager for Developers docs describing the tradeoffs and giving a short decision tree (defaults we ship + opt-ins). Include the ASCII table and bar charts as interim collateral (owner: Priya; due 2028-04-06).
4) Add an observability metric: "proportion of long-waits" = fraction of requests that see upstream wait > 2× median; use to auto-trigger escalation of dedicated slots in a region. (owner: Jonah).

Appendix: sample raw CSV excerpt (columns: scenario,model,pattern,p50,p90,p99,tokens_s,cost_per_k):

short,eager,rwd-7B-fat-multiplex,85,190,420,3400,0.18
short,eager,rwd-13B-quant,55,110,280,1200,0.65
short,eager,rwd-13B-quant-multiplex,110,260,520,2600,0.30
long,chunked,rwd-13B-quant,820,1100,1760,260,0.95
long,chunked,rwd-13B-quant-multiplex,1150,1820,3400,640,0.40
long,chunked,external-70B-multiplex,2400,3900,6700,180,2.90

Notes to self (working bullets):
- We should be careful naming: "multiplex" used internally — call it "pack" in UI? keep internal vs public naming aligned.
- Add a small microdemo in Console that simulates short-turn vs long-turn savings with sliders (very effective for sales).
- Validate p99 impact on single-user sessions (does a single user see >1s pauses?) — telepresence test needed.

End of brief (working draft). Feedback/comments inline encouraged — use Confluence page link above or ping in #console-tooling.
